title: A payoff class
objectives: Model payoffs with a small class hierarchy.
Write a pricer that accepts any payoff through `const Payoff&`.

screens.title: A pricer for calls only
screens.prose: In Python, a pricer calls `payoff(s)` and accepts any object with `__call__`. Here is a first C++ attempt. `value_at` stands in for a pricer: it reads a payoff at one spot. A desk now hands it a put.

lines: double operator()(double s) const { return std::max(s - k, 0.0); }
double operator()(double s) const { return std::max(k - s, 0.0); }
double value_at(const Call& p, double s) { return p(s); }

screens.title: Spot in, pounds out
screens.prose: Look at what the payoffs have in common. Here are a call and a put struck at £100, and a **digital call** that pays £10 when the spot ends above £100. Drag the spot.

derive.caption: Spot £{{spot.x}}: call pays £{{max(spot.x - 100, 0)}}, put £{{max(100 - spot.x, 0)}}, digital £{{spot.x > 100 ? 10 : 0}}

screens.question: Drag the spot to exactly £100. What do the three payoffs pay there?

options.why: You let the digital pay at the strike. It pays only when the spot is strictly above £100, as `spot > strike` says.
The digital has no half payment. At exactly £100 the test `spot > strike` is false, so it pays £0.

options.text: Nothing: a payoff is undefined at its kink
options.why: Each payoff is a rule that gives one number at every spot, kink or not. At £100 all three rules give £0.

hints.text: Watch the caption as the dot reaches £100.
The digital's line jumps at £100. Which dot is filled there?
The filled dot is at £0: the digital pays only above the strike.

feedback.correct: At the strike, all three pay nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption with the spot at exactly £100.

byKey.dig: You let the digital pay at the strike. It pays only when the spot is strictly above £100, as `spot > strike` says.

explain.text: Every payoff answered the same question: given a spot, how many pounds? At exactly £100 all three give £0, so a test there checks that `>` was written, not `>=`. That one question is all a pricer needs to ask.

screens.title: One base, three payoffs
screens.question: A pricer takes `const Payoff& p`. Tap every type whose objects it accepts.

hints.text: Each arrow reads "is a".
`= 0` means `Payoff` gives no body for its function.
A `Call` is a `Payoff`, and so are the other two. No object is ever just a `Payoff`.

feedback.correct: Anything that derives from `Payoff` is accepted.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrows: which types are a `Payoff`?

byKey.payoff: `= 0` makes `Payoff` **abstract**: it has no body for `operator()`, so no `Payoff` object can exist. The reference always refers to a derived object.
byKey.dig: `DigitalCall` derives from `Payoff` too. Every class that derives is accepted, even one written next year.

explain.text: A `Call` is a `Payoff`, so a `const Payoff&` can refer to one. `virtual` means `p(s)` runs the function of the object's real type. `= 0` makes the function **pure virtual** and the base **abstract**: only derived objects exist.

screens.title: Write the payoffs
screens.prose: `Payoff` is loaded. Write `Call`, `Put` and `DigitalCall`. Each stores its strike. `override` asks the compiler to confirm that the function replaces the base's. A digital call pays a fixed `cash` when the spot is strictly above the strike.
screens.question: Write the three classes.

hints.text: Copy `Call` and change one line for `Put`.
The digital needs two members: the strike and the cash.
`return spot > strike_ ? cash_ : 0.0;` inside `double operator()(double spot) const override`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.compile: The compiler stopped. If it says a class is abstract, your `operator()` does not match the base exactly: check `const` and the `double` parameter.
byKey.test-5: A zero-strike call pays the whole spot, 37.5. If yours returns 0, check the order in `spot - strike_`.

explain.text:
Each class answers the base's one question in its own way. `override` makes the compiler check that the signature matches the base, `const` included. A zero-strike call pays the spot itself: it is the share.

```cpp
double operator()(double spot) const override { return spot > strike_ ? cash_ : 0.0; }
```

screens.title: Which function runs
screens.prose: A pricer holds `const Payoff& p` and calls `p(90.0)`. Today `p` refers to an object built as `Put(100.0)`. The tree lists the three `operator()` functions in the program.
screens.question: Tap the function that runs.

hints.text: Which matters here: the type `p` was declared with, or the object it refers to?
This is the declared type. It has no body to run.
`operator()` is `virtual`, so the call follows the object, which was built as a `Put`.

feedback.correct: The object's real type decides, at run time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the object was built as.

byKey.base: You followed the reference's type, `Payoff`. Because `operator()` is `virtual`, the call follows the object, which is a `Put`.
byKey.call: Nothing here is a `Call`. The object `p` refers to was built as `Put(100.0)`.

explain.text: `virtual` makes `p(90.0)` look up the function at run time, by the object's real type. So the put's rule runs and pays £10. This is **virtual dispatch**, and it is why one pricer serves every payoff.

screens.title: A book of payoffs
screens.prose: A position has several **legs**. A `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Payoff>>` holds them: each `unique_ptr` owns one leg of any payoff type. A **straddle** is a call plus a put at one strike. A hidden `straddle(100.0)` builds one.
screens.question: Write `portfolio_payoff`: the sum of every leg's payoff at `spot`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests. Totals are accepted within a relative 1e-9. One book is empty.

hints.text: Loop over the legs. Each one is a pointer: how do you call the object it points to?
Copying a `unique_ptr` is forbidden, so loop by reference.
`for (const auto& leg : legs) total += (*leg)(spot);`

feedback.correct: One loop prices any mix of payoffs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.compile: If the error mentions a deleted copy constructor, your loop copies each `unique_ptr`. Loop by `const auto&`. If it says `leg` cannot be called, write `(*leg)(spot)`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 passes an empty book. Start `total` at 0 and return it unchanged.

explain.text:
`(*leg)` is the payoff the pointer owns, and calling it dispatches by its real type. The loop takes each `unique_ptr` by `const` reference, because a `unique_ptr` cannot be copied. When the vector dies, each `unique_ptr` deletes its leg through `Payoff`'s virtual destructor.

```cpp
for (const auto& leg : legs) total += (*leg)(spot);
```

screens.title: A function that overrides nothing
screens.prose: A colleague's older library has a plain base class: its `operator()` returns 0 unless a payoff replaces it. He adds a put, without `override`.

lines: virtual double operator()(double spot) const { return 0.0; }
double operator()(double spot) { return std::max(k_ - spot, 0.0); }
double value_at(const Payoff& p, double s) { return p(s); }
params.title: main.cpp

screens.question: What does the program print?

options.why: You read lines 6 and 11 as one function. Line 11 has no `const`, so it is a new function, and `value_at` calls line 6's.
Without `override`, nothing asks the compiler to check. A second function with the same name is legal C++.
Nothing goes wrong at run time. The base's function runs and quietly returns 0.

hints.text: Compare line 6 with line 11 word by word.
One of them ends with `const`.
`value_at` holds a `const Payoff&`, so it can call only the `const` function: line 6, which returns 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether line 11 really replaces line 6.

byKey.ten: You read lines 6 and 11 as one function. Line 11 has no `const`, so it is a new function, and `value_at` calls line 6's.

explain.text:
Line 11 lacks `const`, so it adds a second function instead of replacing line 6's, and the put prices at £0. Write `override` on line 11 and the compiler refuses: `only virtual member functions can be marked 'override'`. An abstract base catches it too, at `Put(100.0)`.

```cpp
double operator()(double spot) { ... }                 // new function
double operator()(double spot) const override { ... }  // replaces line 6
```

screens.prose: A payoff can be built from others. Write `Straddle`, a `Payoff` that holds a `Call` and a `Put` at one strike and pays their sum. A pricer then sees one payoff, not two legs. `portfolio_payoff` is loaded.
screens.question: Write `Straddle`'s `operator()`.

hints.text: The members `call_` and `put_` are payoffs already. Call them.
Mark the function `const override`, as the base's is `const`.
`double operator()(double spot) const override { return call_(spot) + put_(spot); }`

feedback.correct: A composite payoff, priced like any other.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

screens.title: Copied into the base
screens.prose: The older library again, with a concrete base. Two helpers read a payoff: one takes it by value, one by reference.

lines: virtual double operator()(double spot) const { return 0.0; }
double operator()(double spot) const override { return std::max(spot - k_, 0.0); }
double by_value(Payoff p, double s) { return p(s); }
double by_ref(const Payoff& p, double s) { return p(s); }
params.title: main.cpp

screens.question: What does the program print?

options.why: You expected the copy to stay a `Call`. `by_value` builds a new `Payoff` from `c`: only the base part is copied, so the base's function runs.
The reference is the one that keeps the `Call`. The copy on line 13 is the one that loses it.
Copying a `Call` into a `Payoff` compiles when the base is concrete. With our abstract base it would not, one more reason to make it abstract.

hints.text: What type is the parameter `p` on line 13?
`Payoff p` is a new object of type `Payoff`.
The copy keeps only `Payoff`'s part of `c`, so line 4's function runs: 0. The reference on line 14 still refers to `c`.

feedback.correct: The copy is a `Payoff`, not a `Call`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what type of object each helper actually holds.

byKey.both: You expected the copy to stay a `Call`. `by_value` builds a new `Payoff` from `c`: only the base part is copied, so the base's function runs.

explain.text: Passing by value builds a fresh `Payoff` from the `Payoff` part of `c`; the strike and the call's function are cut off. This is **slicing**. A reference refers to the original `Call`, so virtual dispatch still works.

screens.question: The desk adds a `Butterfly` payoff. What must change?

options.text: Only a new class, `Butterfly : public Payoff`

options.why: `price` takes `const Payoff&`, so it already accepts any class that derives from `Payoff`.
A base class never names its children. The new class names its base.

options.text: The vector type in every book
options.why: `std::unique_ptr<Payoff>` already owns any derived payoff.

hints.text: Which piece of code mentions `Call` by name?
Only the class itself does. `price` and the books mention `Payoff`.

feedback.correct: New payoffs never touch the pricers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the code that names a particular payoff.

explain.text: The pricer depends only on `Payoff`'s one function. Each new payoff is one new class, and code already written does not change. Python gets this from duck typing at run time; C++ gets it from the base class, checked when it compiles.

screens.title: A capped call for the structuring desk
screens.prose: A structuring desk sells a **capped call** to a client: it pays like a call struck at £100, but never more than £20. The desk's pricers all take `const Payoff&` and must not change. Write the new payoff.
screens.question: Write `CappedCall`'s `operator()`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 8 hidden tests. Payoffs are accepted within a relative 1e-9. One test checks that a capped call equals a call at £100 minus a call at £120.

hints.text: Start from the call's payoff, then limit it.
`std::min` limits from above; `std::max` from below.
`return std::min(std::max(spot - strike_, 0.0), cap_);`

feedback.correct: One new class, and every pricer on the desk can price it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 has the spot at £150. The payoff stops at the cap, £20.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has the spot below the strike. The payoff is 0 there, not negative.

explain.text: `std::min(std::max(spot - strike_, 0.0), cap_)` is the whole job. A capped call equals a call at £100 minus a call at £120, which gives a test against two classes you already trust. A desk's library grows this way: every exotic is one class.

ideas: An abstract base class `Payoff` declares one pure virtual function, `double operator()(double spot) const`. Each payoff derives from it and overrides it.
A pricer takes `const Payoff&`. Virtual dispatch runs the function of the object's real type, so new payoffs never change the pricer.
Own payoffs with `std::unique_ptr<Payoff>`, give the base a virtual destructor, mark overrides with `override`, and never pass a payoff by value.

formula.name: Capped call
formula.note: One class; every pricer prices it unchanged.

summary.trap: A derived function whose signature differs from the base's (a missing `const`) adds a new function instead of overriding. `override` turns that into a compile error.

quiz.question: When `p` goes out of scope, what happens?

options.text: Only `~Payoff` runs, so `weights_` is never freed (formally, undefined behaviour)

options.why: That needs `virtual ~Payoff()`. Without `virtual`, deleting through a `Payoff*` calls only `~Payoff`.
It compiles. Clang can warn about a non-virtual destructor, but the code builds.

options.text: Nothing goes wrong: `unique_ptr` remembers the real type
options.why: `std::unique_ptr<Payoff>` deletes a `Payoff*`. It is `std::shared_ptr` that remembers the type it was made with.

feedback.correct: A base meant for deleting through needs a virtual destructor.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the base's destructor.

explain.text: The deleter calls `delete` on a `Payoff*`, and `~Payoff` is not virtual, so `~Basket` never runs. Its vector leaks, and the standard calls it undefined behaviour. `virtual ~Payoff() = default;` fixes it in one line.

quiz.prose: A book holds `Call(0.0)` and `Put(100.0)`. The spot ends at £92.50.
quiz.question: What does `portfolio_payoff` return, in pounds?

widget.label: Book payoff in pounds
widget.accept: £100: the zero-strike call pays £92.50, the put £7.50.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each leg at £92.50, then add.

byKey.worthless: You priced the zero-strike call at 0. It pays `max(92.5 - 0, 0)`: the whole spot.
byKey.spot: That is the zero-strike call alone. Add the put's £7.50.

explain.text: A zero-strike call pays the spot, so it is the share. With a put at £100 the book pays $\max(S, 100)$, here £100.

quiz.prose: Each line below is a declaration inside `class Put : public Payoff`, with our abstract `Payoff`.
quiz.question: Which declaration fails to compile?

options.why: That matches the base exactly: same parameter, `const`, same return type.
A `const` on a parameter passed by value is not part of the signature, so it still overrides.
Repeating `virtual` is allowed. The signature matches the base.

feedback.correct: Without `const` it overrides nothing, and `override` says so.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each with `virtual double operator()(double spot) const`.

explain.text: The base's function is `const`. A version without `const` is a different function, so `override` makes the compiler refuse it. Without `override` it would compile and never run through a `Payoff&`.

quiz.prose: In Python, `value_at(p, s)` returns `p(s)`. Someone passes an object with no `__call__`. In C++, someone passes a `std::string` to `value_at(const Payoff& p, double s)`.
quiz.question: When is each mistake found?

options.text: Python when the line runs; C++ when the code compiles

options.why: C++ checks argument types at compile time. The program would not be built.
Python checks nothing until it calls `p(s)`; then it raises `TypeError`.
Python raises `TypeError` and C++ refuses to compile. Neither returns a number.

feedback.correct: Duck typing checks late; a base class checks early.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when each language looks at the argument's type.

explain.text: Python's duck typing accepts anything until the call fails at run time. C++ accepts only types that derive from `Payoff`, and it checks before the program exists.
